properties.body:
## Description

The `--port` option for `flask run` accepts any integer with no range validation, leading to confusing behavior:

1. `--port -1` crashes with a raw `OverflowError` traceback instead of a clean usage error
2. `--port 99999` silently starts the server on port 34463 (the OS wraps the value) with zero warning

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
flask run --port -1
# Results in: OverflowError traceback

flask run --port 99999
# Results in: "Running on http://127.0.0.1:34463" (wrong port, no warning)
```

## Expected behavior

Invalid ports should be rejected with a clean usage error. Port 0 should remain allowed (it means "pick any free port").

## Location

`src/flask/cli.py`, the `--port` option is declared with `default=5000` and no type or range check.

## Suggested fix

Use `type=click.IntRange(0, 65535)` on the option so click rejects out-of-range values with a proper usage error.
properties.title: `flask run --port` accepts out-of-range ports without validation

`tests/test_basic.py::test_werkzeug_passthrough_errors` mocks `werkzeug.serving.run_simple` and stores `kwargs.get("passthrough_errors")` in `rv`, but nothing reads `rv` afterwards. Across its 24 parametrized cases it only checks that `app.run()` doesn't raise.

As far as I can see, `Flask.run` no longer sets `passthrough_errors` itself (it passes `**options` through), so the original assertion may have been dropped when that logic was removed. Should the test assert that `passthrough_errors` is not set unless the caller passes it (and that it's forwarded when they do), or be removed? I can send a PR for whichever you prefer.

(Found with [hollowtest](https://github.com/jeffev/hollowtest), a checker for tests that cannot fail.)

properties.body:
### Describe the bug

`Config.from_prefixed_env()` raises an unhandled `TypeError` when environment variables contain both a scalar configuration key and a nested configuration key sharing the same prefix.

The method supports nested configuration using double underscores (`__`). However, when a scalar key is processed first, the nested key attempts to assign into that scalar value instead of a dictionary, causing the method to crash.

### To reproduce

```python
import os
from flask import Config

config = Config(root_path=".")

os.environ["FLASK_TEST"] = "hello"
os.environ["FLASK_TEST__INNER"] = "world"

config.from_prefixed_env("FLASK")
```

### Expected behavior

The configuration loader should handle conflicting scalar and nested keys gracefully, either by resolving the conflict consistently or raising a clear, intentional configuration error.

### Actual behavior

The method raises an unhandled exception:

```text
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
```

The exception occurs at:

```python
current[tail] = value
```

in `src/flask/config.py`, inside `Config.from_prefixed_env()`.

### Environment

- Flask: 3.2.0.dev0 (local development checkout)
- Python: 3.12.10
- Operating system: Windows

### Additional evidence

The issue was reproduced using a minimal standalone Python script. The full Flask test suite passes (491 passed, 3 skipped), indicating that this edge case is not currently covered by the existing tests.
properties.title: [rejected AI] Config.from_prefixed_env raises TypeError when scalar and nested environment variables share a prefix

Two code examples in [docs/errorhandling.rst](https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/main/docs/errorhandling.rst) don't work as written:

- def user_api(user_id): takes a `user_id` argument, but the route `/api/user` has no URL variable, so Flask raises `TypeError` when the view is called. The parameter should be removed, the value comes from the query string
- The `user_profile` and `user_api` examples call request.arg.get(...). Request has no `arg` attribute, so this raises `AttributeError`. It should be `request.args`

Environment:

- Python version: 3.14.4
- Flask version: 3.2.0.dev0 (commit d086db8)

The 3.2 changelog says:

> Many ``Flask`` methods involved in request dispatch now take the current
> ``AppContext`` as the first parameter. If subclasses were overriding these
> methods, the old signature is detected, shows a deprecation warning, and will
> continue to work during the deprecation period.

As far as I can tell `update_template_context` isn't covered by that. Its
signature did change:

- 3.1.3: `def update_template_context(self, context: dict[str, t.Any]) -> None:`
- main: `def update_template_context(self, ctx: AppContext, context: dict[str, t.Any]) -> None:`

and `templating.py` now calls `app.update_template_context(ctx, context)`. But
the tuple in `Flask.__init_subclass__` (app.py, around line 258) has 12 methods
in it and `update_template_context` isn't one of them. The list you posted on
#5815 has 13, so I'm guessing it just got missed.

So a subclass that overrides it the old way gets no warning and no wrapping:

```python
from flask import Flask, render_template_string


class App(Flask):
    def update_template_context(self, context):
        context["x"] = "y"


app = App(__name__)


@app.route("/")
def index():
    return render_template_string("{{ x }}")


app.test_client().get("/")
```

```
  File "flask/templating.py", line 125, in _render
    app.update_template_context(ctx, context)
TypeError: App.update_template_context() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given
```

The request comes back as a 500 and no DeprecationWarning is raised. The same
code returns 200 on 3.1.3.

One other thing I ran into while testing this, which is probably worth its own
issue: overrides that do use the new signature but don't spell it exactly the
way the check expects are picked up as the old signature instead. Renaming the
parameter (`def dispatch_request(self, context)`) or annotating it as
`ctx: AppContext | None` makes the ctx argument get stripped, so those fail
with a TypeError as well. Same with `finalize_request` annotated
`typing.Optional[AppContext]`. Happy to file that separately if you'd rather.

`app.register_blueprint(bp, host="a.localhost")` doesn't error and doesn't do anything, because the `host` kwarg goes into `**options` and is never read, so every rule of the blueprint is registered hostless.
I checked `flask/(sansio)/blueprints.py` in 2.3.3, 3.1.3 and current `main`: `host` has never been read on that path, in any release. It just does not exist for blueprints themselves.

Depending on the app config this fails in two opposite ways, both silent.

```python
import flask

a_bp = flask.Blueprint("a_bp", __name__)
b_bp = flask.Blueprint("b_bp", __name__)


@a_bp.route("/")
def a_home():
    return "a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only"


@b_bp.route("/")
def b_home():
    return "b_bp view: meant for b.localhost only"


def probe(app):
    client = app.test_client()
    for host in ("a.localhost", "b.localhost", "evil.example"):
        r = client.get("/", headers={"Host": host})
        body = repr(r.get_data(as_text=True)) if r.status_code == 200 else ""
        print(f"GET /  Host: {host:14} -> {r.status_code} {body}")


app = flask.Flask(__name__, static_folder=None)
app.register_blueprint(a_bp, host="a.localhost")
app.register_blueprint(b_bp, host="b.localhost")

host_matched = flask.Flask(__name__, host_matching=True, static_folder=None)
host_matched.register_blueprint(a_bp, host="a.localhost")
host_matched.register_blueprint(b_bp, host="b.localhost")

print("=== host_matching=False (default) ===")
probe(app)
print("=== host_matching=True ===")
probe(host_matched)
```

Output, Flask 3.1.3 / Werkzeug 3.1.8 / Python 3.12:

```
=== host_matching=False (default) ===
GET /  Host: a.localhost    -> 200 'a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only'
GET /  Host: b.localhost    -> 200 'a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only'
GET /  Host: evil.example   -> 200 'a_bp view: meant for a.localhost only'
=== host_matching=True ===
GET /  Host: a.localhost    -> 404
GET /  Host: b.localhost    -> 404
GET /  Host: evil.example   -> 404
```

With the default app the host isn't part of matching at all, so a_bp's hostless rule answers every hostname and b_bp is registered but unreachable. This is a cross-host leak with no error, no warning, and nothing for a type checker to catch, since `**options` accepts anything.
While with `host_matching=True` it flips the other way: a hostless rule matches nothing, so everything 404s.

For contrast, `flask.Blueprint("a", __name__, host=...)` does raise a `TypeError` because it accepts some kwargs but not `host` (since it has no **options catch-all).

Some context: #5411 was closed as not planned on the basis that `register_blueprint(a_bp, host=...)` was the existing way to do this, and the example posted in reply there was never answered. Running that example is what led me here. I also posted a shorter version of this on discussion #5413 yesterday, which was removed when the discussion was closed. I'm sorry I revived a very old discussion, and that it was necessary to remove the comment. The point of it was to confirm that the report still reproduces and to contribute a tested example.
I hope that opening this issue is the correct way to proceed now.

As for what to do about it: given how subtle the interaction between `SERVER_NAME`, `host_matching` and `subdomain_matching` has historically been (see for example #5553 and the fix in #5634), I can understand not wanting to grow that API surface.
The minimal fix would then be to reject `host` loudly in `BlueprintSetupState`, same as the constructor does.

But if honoring it is on the table instead, the gap it would fill is easy to state: having `host=` for blueprints too, not only route decorators. Today, pinning more than one route to a host means repeating `host=` on each of them (and not missing any), or subclassing. To me, the missing blueprint-level scope is a feature gap, but a documented per-route recipe would already be an improvement.

Either way, the docs gap stands on its own: the blueprints page documents subdomains at blueprint scope but never says a word about hosts, which is part of why I thought `host=` was supported. I can contribute a recipe for pinning a blueprint to one host with today's API, something like this (simplified from what I run in production, together with `host_matching=True`):

```python
class HostBlueprint(flask.Blueprint):
    def __init__(self, *args, host: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._host = host

    def add_url_rule(self, rule, endpoint=None, view_func=None, **options):
        options.setdefault("host", self._host)
        return super().add_url_rule(rule, endpoint, view_func, **options)
```

I can send a PR for whichever direction sounds right to you.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13
- Flask version: 3.1.3

properties.body: That has nothing to do with Flask, you need to configure Waitress, or the HTTP server in front of Waitress.
Yes, that's why it's already written in the Werkzeug docs to configure it on the server instead. You need to add that to the Flask docs as well.

The Werkzeug docs were updated to say what they say now [approximately a month ago](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/pull/3251). I don't constantly go back and forth keeping the two in sync.

`MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH` should not be _avoided_. In fact, the docs as written in Werkzeug wouldn't help you either. They say that `max_content_length` must be set _somewhere_. The problem you're reporting is that Waitress buffers the response before it gets to the application. Because of that Waitress behavior, the max length can only be configured there, not further down the stack.

So I suppose what the docs need to say is "be aware of the stack you're using, how each tool interacts with requests and responses, and how to configure each one appropriately." That seems like such general advice, and applies to everything not just `max_content_length`, so I don't think it's worth saying specifically there.

Repo: pallets/flask · base: 2a8a38b051fc248865730bf3511bf2e2ea325e81 ("support query in methodview") · branch: charles-fix-flask

## Title

MethodView: register only callable attributes as HTTP methods

## Body

`MethodView.__init_subclass__` builds `cls.methods` with `hasattr(cls, key)` for every
name in `http_method_funcs`, and `dispatch_request` then does `getattr(self, request.method.lower())`
followed by `assert meth is not None`. 2a8a38b added `"query"` to that set, so any existing
`MethodView` subclass that carries a non-callable `query` attribute (for example a
`query = Model.query` shortcut, or `query = None` as a placeholder) now advertises `QUERY` in
`Allow` and answers a `QUERY` request with a 500 (`AssertionError: Unimplemented method 'QUERY'`)
where it returned 405 before. The mechanism predates this change and applies equally to
`get`/`post`/..., but `query` is a far more common data attribute name than the other verbs.

This change switches the detection to `callable(getattr(cls, key, None))`, so data attributes
never register a method; a `def query(self)` still maps to `QUERY` as intended. Reproduction:
`class Item(MethodView): query = None; def get(self): ...` → before: `Item.methods == {"GET", "QUERY"}`,
`QUERY /` → 500; after: `{"GET"}`, `QUERY /` → 405. A test pins this, and CHANGES.rst gains a line
for the new `MethodView`/`query` mapping and for the callable check.

Not covered: a real helper *method* named `query` with a different signature is still registered
(it is callable); that would need a signature check or an explicit opt-in and is a design call for
the maintainers.

## Severity

Low. Backward-compat regression limited to `MethodView` subclasses with a non-callable `query`
attribute, and only for clients that send `QUERY`. No data exposure; the effect is a 500 instead
of a 405 and a misleading `Allow` header.

## Verification

- `uv run --group tests pytest tests/test_views.py -k non_callable` fails on 2a8a38b (test-before.log) and passes with the fix.
- Full suite: 495 passed (test-after.log).
- Upstream `src/flask/views.py` on `main` was byte-identical to this case head at the time of writing.

## Description
‘add_url_rule’ correctly raises an error when an endpoint already exists and you try to register a different view function with the same endpoint.

However, after you catch the error and continue running the code, the URL you tried to add (/b, for example) still exists. When a user requests /b, it is routed to the view function that was already registered for that endpoint, rather than the new view function whose registration failed.

## Example

```python
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

def first():
    return "first"

def second():
    return "second"

app.add_url_rule("/a", endpoint="same", view_func=first)

try:
    app.add_url_rule("/b", endpoint="same", view_func=second)
except AssertionError as e:
    print(e)

client = app.test_client()

print(client.get("/a").status_code, client.get("/a").data)
print(client.get("/b").status_code, client.get("/b").data)
```

### Expected Result

```text
View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same
200 b'first'
404 ...
```

### Actual Result

```text
View function mapping is overwriting an existing endpoint function: same
200 b'first'
200 b'first'
```

I think Flask correctly rejects the view-function overwrite, but the failed registration has already added the URL rule.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.11.2
- Flask version: 3.1.3

## Summary

Multiple security vulnerabilities in Flask: CRITICAL code execution via exec() in config.py, HIGH path traversal in 5 locations.

## Vulnerabilities Found

1. **CRITICAL** `config.py:209` - Code Execution via exec() in from_pyfile
   exec(compile(config_file.read(), filename, "exec"), d.__dict__) executes arbitrary Python code from a file.

2. **HIGH** `config.py:204` - Path Traversal in from_pyfile
   filename = os.path.join(self.root_path, filename) without sanitization. Absolute paths bypass root_path.

3. **HIGH** `config.py:290` - Path Traversal in from_file
   Same os.path.join pattern without validation.

4. **HIGH** `app.py:441` - Path Traversal in open_resource
   path = os.path.join(self.root_path, resource) without path validation.

5. **HIGH** `app.py:463` - Path Traversal in open_instance_resource
   Same pattern.

6. **HIGH** `blueprints.py:123` - Path Traversal in open_resource
   os.path.join without traversal protection.

7. **MEDIUM** `cli.py:1023` - Code Execution via eval() in shell_command
   eval(compile(f.read(), startup, "exec")) on PYTHONSTARTUP env var.

## Recommended Fix

1. Use werkzeug.utils.safe_join for all path operations
2. Validate that resolved paths stay within intended directories
3. Document/document-warn on exec/eval usage in config loading

## Note
Several of these are documented Flask features (loading config from Python files is designed to exec code). However, the path traversal combined with env-var-configurable filenames may not be intended.

Fixes #6093 where IPv6 addresses (e.g. `[::1]:8080` or `http://[::1]:8000/`) were parsed incorrectly using `.partition(":")`, causing string splits on colons inside IPv6 host brackets.

## Description

When a client disconnects mid-stream, the WSGI server abandons the body
iterator. The generator is later finalized by the garbage collector, often
on a **different thread** than the one that pushed the context.

`ctx.pop()` raises `RuntimeError` because `_cv_app.get(None)` returns `None`
on the GC thread. The context stays "stuck" on the original worker thread,
and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for subsequent requests on that thread.

## Fix

Replace `with ctx:` with manual `ctx.push()` / `ctx.pop()` in the
`stream_with_context` generator. Wrap `pop()` in a try/except that catches
`RuntimeError` and resets the context state (`_push_count` and `_cv_token`)
to prevent thread pool poisoning.

## Related

- #5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views
- #5804 covers teardown ordering in the 3.1.2 rewrite

Closes #6123

properties.body: Besides being AI generated, which is against our policy, this introduces extreme inefficiency due to pushing and popping the context on every loop.

`stream_with_context` pushes the request's contexts onto whichever thread iterates the response body, and pops them only if the generator completes or is closed on that same thread. When a client disconnects mid-stream, the server abandons the body iterator and GC finalizes it later — often on a different thread. That cross-context pop fails (`LookupError`/`ValueError` from `ContextVar.reset`, swallowed as "Exception ignored in ..."), and the app context stays current on the worker thread.

Because `RequestContext.push` reuses an ambient app context of the same app, every later request on that pooled thread runs under the stuck context and `teardown_appcontext` never fires for it. Anything keyed to the app context then leaks once per thread for the life of the process — with Flask-SQLAlchemy that is one connection held idle-in-transaction per poisoned thread, with nothing in the logs.

Related: #5774 fixed the same cross-context token failure for async views; #5804 covers teardown ordering in the 3.1.2 rewrite. Neither covers the abandonment case. The docs mention that headers/session need care with `stream_with_context`, but not that a disconnect can leave the context stuck on the thread — a warning there would be helpful even if the behavior itself is hard to change.

## Reproduction

One long-lived "worker" thread serves two requests; the abandoned body iterator is GC-finalized on the main thread in between (in real deployments the reference is dropped by server machinery outside the worker — servers may never call `close()` on the iterator after a disconnect):

```python
import gc
import queue
import threading

from flask import Flask, Response, stream_with_context
from flask.globals import _cv_app

app = Flask(__name__)
teardowns = []

@app.teardown_appcontext
def note_teardown(exc):
    teardowns.append(threading.current_thread().name)

@app.route("/stream")
def stream():
    def gen():
        for i in range(100):
            yield f"chunk{i}\n"
    return Response(stream_with_context(gen()))

@app.route("/plain")
def plain():
    return "ok"

abandoned = queue.Queue()   # holds the dropped iterator, like server machinery
step2 = threading.Event()

def worker():
    # --- request A: streaming response, client disconnects after one chunk ---
    with app.test_request_context("/stream"):
        rv = app.full_dispatch_request()
    body = iter(rv.response)
    next(body)   # first chunk: stream_with_context pushes app+request ctx HERE
    abandoned.put((body, rv))   # server-side reference outlives the request
    del body, rv
    print("A: ambient ctx after abandonment:", _cv_app.get(None))

    step2.wait()  # main thread GC-finalizes the generator meanwhile

    # --- request B: any later request on this pooled worker thread ---
    print("B: ambient ctx at request start:", _cv_app.get(None))
    teardowns.clear()
    with app.test_request_context("/plain"):    # reuses the ambient ctx of the
        app.full_dispatch_request()             # same app -> no fresh app ctx
    print("B: teardown_appcontext ran for B:", bool(teardowns))
    print("B: ambient ctx after B finished:", _cv_app.get(None))

t = threading.Thread(target=worker, name="wsgi-worker-0")
t.start()

abandoned.get()          # take the reference, then drop it on the MAIN thread
gc.collect()             # generator finalized here -> cross-context pop fails
step2.set()
t.join()
```

Output (Flask 3.1.3, Python 3.13):

```
Exception ignored in: <generator object stream_with_context.<locals>.generator at 0x...>
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../flask/helpers.py", line 130, in generator
    with app_ctx, req_ctx:
  File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 284, in __exit__
    self.pop(exc_value)
  File ".../flask/ctx.py", line 264, in pop
    ctx = _cv_app.get()
LookupError: <ContextVar name='flask.app_ctx' at 0x...>
A: ambient ctx after abandonment: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
B: ambient ctx at request start: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
B: teardown_appcontext ran for B: False
B: ambient ctx after B finished: <flask.ctx.AppContext object at 0x10b49c830>
```

## Expected behavior

Request B runs under its own app context and `teardown_appcontext` fires when it finishes. Instead it silently runs under request A's leaked context, teardown never runs, and the thread stays poisoned indefinitely.

Environment:

- Python version: 3.13 (also reproduced on 3.11)
- Flask version: 3.1.3. The `main` branch (3.2-dev, post-#5639 merged context) looks affected as well: `stream_with_context` there enters the single context via `with ctx:` around the priming `yield None`, so the context is pushed at creation and only exited when the generator completes or is closed.

The example seems to require "server-side reference outlives the request", which seems extremely unusual. You're deliberately moving a reference from one thread to another, then reporting that the references act weird.

I would really prefer an example that uses a plain flask app and actual requests, rather than trying to simulate a bunch of stuff. There's so much complexity in the example right now that I'm having a hard time following it.

> the server abandons the body iterator and GC finalizes it later

This seems like something to report to the server doing this? They should be calling `close` on the iterator if it has that method. Otherwise they're creating an unclosed resource, something Python has been getting noisier and noisier about with warnings. If you look at Werkzeug's dev server and various app running functions, they all do this.

The app where I ran into this issue is an LLM gateway streaming chat responses from a generator that uses flask + SQLAlchemy/Postgres behind uvicorn (via a2wsgi). Under load I was slowly leaking 20–100 Postgres connections a day until I had to restart. 

 The trap: the streaming generator held a Flask app/request context across its yields, and a2wsgi iterates the response body on a reused thread-pool thread. When a client disconnected mid-stream the generator was abandoned, the context was never popped, and SQLAlchemy's per-context session teardown never ran. The database connection was stuck in "idle in transaction" (which I reaped before I found the issue by setting the postgresql idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 10min). Every later request that landed on that same thread reused the still-current context, so its session teardown never ran either. Each one quietly leaked another connection, which resulting the app loosing connections in the pool slowely and eventually crash, not immediatly.

> The trap:

import socket
import threading
import time

from flask.globals import _cv_app
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
from sqlalchemy.orm import scoped_session, sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.pool import QueuePool
from a2wsgi import WSGIMiddleware
import uvicorn

PORT = 8765
POOL_SIZE = 30

# sqlite database with connection pool
engine = create_engine(
    "sqlite:///./mydb.db",
    poolclass=QueuePool,
    pool_size=POOL_SIZE,
    max_overflow=0,
    connect_args={"check_same_thread": False},
)

# my flask app
app = Flask(__name__)
asgi_app = WSGIMiddleware(app, workers=16)

# code to keep track of connections
def _scope():
    ctx = _cv_app.get(None)
    return id(ctx) if ctx is not None else None

Session = scoped_session(sessionmaker(bind=engine), scopefunc=_scope)

@app.teardown_appcontext
def _cleanup(exc):
    # Flask runs this when the app context is popped. If the context is stranded

# start serving the data
def _serve():
    uvicorn.run(asgi_app, host="127.0.0.1", port=PORT, log_level="critical")

    s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", PORT), timeout=5)

    time.sleep(2)

    for batch in range(1, 6):
        threads = [threading.Thread(target=_abort_request) for _ in range(20)]
        for t in threads:

        for t in threads:

        time.sleep(1)
        checked_out = engine.pool.checkedout()
        live_sessions = len(Session.registry.registry)
        print(f"{batch:>6} {checked_out:>12} {live_sessions:>14}")

    print(

        else "\nno leak — connections all returned"
    )
    checked_out = engine.pool.checkedout()
    live_sessions = len(Session.registry.registry)
    print(f"{batch:>6} {checked_out:>12} {live_sessions:>14}")

Sorry, that's still way too much. I can't debug a2wsgi, I'm not familiar with it at all, if you think it's causing issues then report that to them. Use Flask's dev server, it's threaded. It doesn't seem like sqlalchemy is necessary at all to demonstrate that contexts aren't cleaned up.

I've been looking into this for hours now, and as far as I can tell the problem is that something is not closing the response. Flask _can't_ do that, it's in the server's control at that point.

In your first example, you're never calling `body.close()` when the "connection" is disconnected, and you're deliberately moving it somewhere with a different `contextvar`. If you call `body.close()` in the worker (not in some other thread) it works fine.

In your second example, presumably a2wsgi isn't handling client disconnects correctly, it needs to detect them and close the response.

It seems like Flask is managing the context correctly but your server is not handling disconnects correctly. How should a2wsgi do that? I don't know, but I'd suggest you report it to them.

## Summary

`Config.from_prefixed_env` can raise an uncaught `TypeError` when an environment
variable creates a scalar configuration value and another variable later tries
to use that same value as a nested mapping.

### Reproduction

With Flask's development source at commit
`6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58`:

```bash
FLASK_FOO=bar FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz python - <<'PY'
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)
app.config.from_prefixed_env()
PY
```

The call raises:

```text
TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
```

### What happens

`from_prefixed_env` processes matching environment variables in sorted order.
The first variable sets `config["FOO"]` to the string `"bar"`. When processing
`FLASK_FOO__BAR`, the nested traversal reaches this value and then attempts to
assign through it:

```python
current = current[part]
...
current[tail] = value
```

The intermediate value is a string rather than a mapping, so configuration
loading fails with a low-level `TypeError`.

Relevant source at the reproduction commit:
<https://github.com/pallets/flask/blob/6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58/src/flask/config.py#L172-L183>

### Expected behavior

Configuration loading should not fail with an implementation-level
`TypeError` for a prefix collision. The behavior should be defined and
deterministic, for example by rejecting the conflicting configuration with a
clear error, or by documenting and implementing precedence/merge semantics.

### Impact

An application can fail during startup or configuration initialization when
environment variables are assembled from multiple sources and a scalar key
and nested key happen to share a prefix. This can be difficult to diagnose
because the error does not identify the conflicting environment variables.

### Suggested regression test

Add a test covering both `FLASK_FOO=bar` and `FLASK_FOO__BAR=baz`, and assert the
chosen behavior for the scalar/nested conflict. If the intended behavior is to
reject the configuration, the error should identify the conflicting path.

### Environment

- Flask source commit: `6a2f545bfd8ed31e19066a299296917e034aca58`
- Flask version: `3.2.0.dev`
- Python: `3.13.13`
- Reproduction is independent of operating system semantics because it only
  relies on the environment-variable traversal logic.

I have not assigned a CWE classification. This is reported as a configuration
robustness and error-handling issue rather than a nullability finding.

## Fix IPv6 address parsing in `session_transaction`

Fixes part of #6093.

### Problem

Two places in Flask use `.partition(":")` to parse host:port strings, but IPv6 addresses like `[::1]:8000` contain multiple colons, so `.partition(":")` splits at the wrong position:

1. **`session_transaction` in `src/flask/testing.py`** — `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` returns `"["` instead of `"[::1]"` for IPv6 hosts. This breaks cookie domain extraction during session transactions with IPv6 base URLs.
2. **`Flask.run()` in `src/flask/app.py`** — `server_name.partition(":")` incorrectly parses `SERVER_NAME` when it contains an IPv6 address (e.g., `[::1]:8080`).

### Fix applied in this PR (testing.py)

Replaced `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` with `urlsplit(ctx.request.host_url).hostname or "localhost"`. The `host_url` property includes the scheme (e.g., `http://[::1]:8000`), so `urlsplit` can correctly parse the hostname from IPv6 addresses. The `urlsplit` import already exists in `testing.py`.

### Fix still needed (app.py)

The `run()` method in `src/flask/app.py` also needs the same fix. The change would be:

```python
# In imports, add:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

# In run() method, replace:
sn_host, _, sn_port = server_name.partition(":")
# With:
sn_url = urlsplit(f"//{server_name}")
sn_host = sn_url.hostname
sn_port = sn_url.port

# And change:
port = int(sn_port)
# To:
port = sn_port  # sn_port is already int | None from urlsplit
```

This follows the same approach used in the [Werkzeug fix](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug) for the same issue.

### Test added

Added `test_session_transaction_ipv6` to `tests/test_testing.py` which verifies that session transactions work correctly with IPv6 base URLs:

```python
def test_session_transaction_ipv6(app):
    base_url = "http://[::1]:8000/"
    client = app.test_client()

    @app.get("/")
    def index():
        return str(flask.session.get("value"))

    with client.session_transaction(base_url=base_url) as sess:
        sess["value"] = 42

    assert client.get("/", base_url=base_url).text == "42"
```

This test fails without the fix (raises an error or returns incorrect results) and passes with the fix.

`jsonify` serialises `float("nan")` and `float("inf")` as the bare literals `NaN` and `Infinity`. Those are not valid JSON (RFC 8259 allows only decimal numbers), so the response is served as `application/json` but cannot be parsed by a strict parser, including the browser's `JSON.parse`.

This inherits from `json.dumps`, whose `allow_nan` defaults to `True`. `DefaultJSONProvider` sets `default`, `ensure_ascii` and `sort_keys`, but never touches `allow_nan`, so the permissive default applies.

The path to it is ordinary: any average, ratio or division that can meet an empty input produces `nan` without anything looking wrong on the server.

Replication:

```python
from flask import Flask, jsonify

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/stats")
def stats():
    values = []
    mean = sum(values) / len(values) if values else float("nan")
    return jsonify({"count": len(values), "mean": mean})

with app.test_client() as c:
    r = c.get("/stats")
    print(r.headers["Content-Type"])      # application/json
    print(r.get_data(as_text=True))       # {"count":0,"mean":NaN}
```

The response advertises `application/json` with a 200, but the body is not JSON:

```python
import json
json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}')      # accepted, Python is permissive by default
json.loads('{"count":0,"mean":NaN}',
           parse_constant=lambda x: (_ for _ in ()).throw(ValueError(x)))
# ValueError: NaN     <- what a strict parser, and JSON.parse in a browser, does
```

So the failure surfaces in the client rather than the server, which makes it awkward to trace back.

Expected: either the same behaviour with it documented, or serialisation raises so the problem shows up server-side, where `ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan` names the cause immediately.

There is currently no class attribute for this, although the plumbing already works, since `dumps` forwards `**kwargs` to `json.dumps`:

```python
app.json.dumps({"a": float("nan")}, allow_nan=False)
# ValueError: Out of range float values are not JSON compliant: nan
```

`DefaultJSONProvider` exposes `sort_keys`, `ensure_ascii` and `compact` as class attributes, so an `allow_nan` attribute alongside them would fit the existing pattern and let applications choose, without changing the default for anyone. I could not find `NaN` mentioned in the `DefaultJSONProvider` or `flask.json.dumps` docstrings, so at minimum a documentation note seems worthwhile.

Happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer, an `allow_nan` provider attribute or just the docs.

Environment:

- Python 3.14
- Flask 3.1.3
- Werkzeug 3.1.8

In `wsgi_app`, the call to `response(environ, start_response)` sits outside the inner `try/except` that catches dispatch errors. When this call raises (for example, a streaming response body fails or the client disconnects mid-delivery), the `error` variable remains `None`. The `finally` block then calls `ctx.pop(error)` with `error=None`, so all `teardown_request` functions receive `exc=None` instead of the actual exception. This silently discards the error, making it impossible for teardown logic to make informed cleanup decisions (such as rolling back a database transaction versus committing).

The fix wraps `response(environ, start_response)` in a `try/except BaseException` that captures the error into the `error` variable before re-raising. The `finally` block then passes the correct exception to `ctx.pop(error)`. Using `BaseException` ensures that `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`, and other non-`Exception` throwables during WSGI response delivery are also captured. The exception is always re-raised after capture — it is never swallowed or handled, preserving the existing contract that `wsgi_app` propagates unexpected errors to the WSGI server.

A regression test is added that creates a `Response` subclass whose `__call__` raises `RuntimeError`, registers a `teardown_request` handler, and asserts that the handler receives the `RuntimeError` instance. This test fails on the unpatched code (teardown receives `None`) and passes with the fix. The full Flask test suite (492 tests) passes with no regressions.

## Description

Fixes incorrect host parsing for IPv6 addresses in two locations.

## Problem

Two places used `.partition(":")` to split host:port, which breaks for IPv6 addresses like `[::1]:8000` because the colon inside the bracket notation is not the host:port separator.

1. **testing.py:180** - `ctx.request.host.partition(":")[0]` returns `[::1` instead of `::1` for IPv6 host headers
2. **app.py:724** - `server_name.partition(":")` returns `[::1` as host and `8000]` as port for IPv6 SERVER_NAME

## Fix

- **testing.py**: Use bracket-aware parsing - if host starts with `[`, extract hostname between brackets; otherwise use existing partition logic
- **app.py**: Use bracket-aware parsing - if server_name starts with `[`, find the `]` bracket and parse port after it; otherwise use existing partition logic

## Testing

Added comprehensive test cases covering:
- IPv4 with port: `127.0.0.1:8000`
- IPv6 with port: `[::1]:8000`
- IPv4 without port: `localhost`
- IPv6 without port: `[::1]`
- IPv6 full address: `[2001:db8::1]:8080`

All tests pass.

Closes #6093

pytest 9.1 removed the private `notset` sentinel from `_pytest.monkeypatch` (now `NOTSET` in `_pytest.compat`). The test suite imported `notset` and directly manipulated `monkeypatch._setitem`, causing a collection-time crash with pytest 9.1+.

- **`tests/conftest.py`**: Use `pytest.MonkeyPatch()` + `delenv()` instead of `_pytest.monkeypatch.MonkeyPatch()` + `notset`. The `_reset_os_environ` fixture now also cleans up dotenv test keys (`FOO`, `BAR`, `SPAM`, `HAM`, `EGGS`) that `load_dotenv()` sets directly, bypassing monkeypatch's tracking.
- **`tests/test_cli.py`**: Replace `from _pytest.monkeypatch import notset` and `monkeypatch._setitem.append((os.environ, item, notset))` with `monkeypatch.delenv(item, raising=False)`.

### Development Versions CI: deprecated werkzeug API

werkzeug main (3.2 dev) deprecated `parse_cache_control_header` and `parse_set_header` (removal in 3.3). With `filterwarnings = ["error"]`, the `DeprecationWarning` crashes test collection.

- **`tests/test_blueprints.py`**: Use `ResponseCacheControl.from_header()` instead of `parse_cache_control_header()`, with `hasattr` fallback to the old function for `werkzeug < 3.2`.
- **`tests/test_views.py`**: Use `HeaderSet.from_header()` instead of `parse_set_header()`, with `hasattr` fallback for `werkzeug < 3.2`.

### Minimum Versions CI: click ParamType subscripting

`click.ParamType` became subscriptable in click 8.2, but Flask declares `click>=8.1.3` as minimum. `class CertParamType(click.ParamType[t.Any])` crashes on click 8.1.3 with `TypeError: type 'ParamType' is not subscriptable`.

- **`src/flask/cli.py`**: Use `click.ParamType` directly as the base class — the generic parameter is only for type checkers and has no runtime effect.

- [x] Full test suite passes on pytest 9.1.1 + werkzeug 3.1.0 + click 8.1.3 (133 passed for affected modules)
- [x] Test suite crashes without the pytest fix (ImportError on `notset`)

## Description

[RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc10008/) (June 2026) standardizes
the `QUERY` HTTP method: a safe, idempotent request method that carries content
in the request body (standardizing the "POST for a read-only query with a large
body" workaround used by GraphQL and REST search endpoints).

Flask already routes and dispatches arbitrary method names, so this adds the
idiomatic ergonomics that mirror the existing
`get`/`post`/`put`/`delete`/`patch` shortcuts:

- `Scaffold.query()` registers a route with `methods=["QUERY"]`, inherited by
  both `Flask` and `Blueprint`.
- `"query"` is added to `views.http_method_funcs`, so `MethodView` dispatches a
  `QUERY` request to a `query` handler.

Higher-level RFC 10008 features (the `Accept-Query` header, server-assigned
query-result URIs, caching semantics) are application/Werkzeug concerns and are
intentionally out of scope.

## Summary

`SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` is documented and implemented as a list of old signing keys. If an app accidentally configures it as a scalar string or bytes value, the session interface currently calls `keys.extend(fallbacks)`, which expands the value into one-character or one-byte fallback keys before constructing the `itsdangerous` serializer.

This rejects scalar `str` and `bytes` fallback values before building the key list, while preserving the existing list-based key rotation behavior.

## Security impact

For an affected app using signed cookie sessions, a misconfigured value such as `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS = "old-secret"` could make Flask accept cookies signed with a single-character fallback key such as `"o"`. I verified the pre-fix behavior with a cookie signed using `"o"`; the session loaded successfully when `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` was a string. After this change, the same request raises a configuration `TypeError` instead of accepting the forged session.

This can also happen through environment configuration if a value is supplied as a plain string instead of JSON/list syntax.

The Blueprint constructor rejects a name that contains a dot, because dots are the separator used for nested blueprint names and endpoints. The name can also be overridden at registration with the name option, but that path was not validated, so a dotted name was silently accepted.

A dotted registered name is then treated as a nested hierarchy. For example register_blueprint(bp, name="a.b") registers the blueprint as "a.b" while request.blueprints reports ["a.b", "a"], referencing a parent scope "a" that was never registered. Endpoints and blueprint scoped lookups (error handlers, url_for, request.blueprint) walk that non existent scope.

Apply the same check to the name option so both paths raise the same ValueError. Added a test alongside the existing constructor test.

properties.body: @davidism, how would you feel if I took the big cannon here and replaced all the private pytest API use? I'm thinking of making `_standard_os_environ` test-scoped and removing `_reset_os_environ` (I don't think the optimization to make it session scoped is really worth it), and making `test_cli` use `delitem(..., raising=False)`.
Actually, I don't really understand why it's done like that. FWIU it first unsets all envvars once, then unsets them after every test… rather than unsetting them before every test?
I only vaguely remember implementing all that environ stuff. I'll need to investigate what it was about, there was definitely a reason at the time.
Do you think it would be sufficient that I try if tests pass without it?

Yeah, but try on Linux and Windows if you can. I think it might have had to do with running tests while also having an example app running (like when fixing a bug), so `FLASK_APP` was set and messing things up?

Okay, I think I've found the non-obvious difference: the logic as it stands now always restores the environment variables to their original state. Plain `monkeypatch.delenv(...)` only restores the original value if the envvar was set; if it wasn't and the test sets it, it isn't unset afterwards, i.e.:

```python
import os

def test_foo(monkeypatch):
  monkeypatch.delenv("FOO", False)
  os.environ["FOO"] = "bar"

def test_bar():
  assert os.environ.get("FOO") is None
```

will fail if `FOO` is unset, since `test_foo()` will leave it set as `bar`.

That said, the tests are broken anyway, given that they fail if `FOO` is set in the calling environment already, so I'm not sure if cleaning up the environment after the tests setting `FOO` really makes sense. In the end, it only hides the actual issue with other tests relying on `FOO` not being set.
Tracked the origin of these fixtures to #2589 and PR #2592. It was because I had an example `FLASK_APP` set in the environment when running the tests, which the tests didn't expect.

## Bug

`Config.from_prefixed_env` silently crashes with an opaque `TypeError` when a flat env var and a nested env var share the same config key prefix.

**Root cause:** env vars are loaded in `sorted()` order, so `FLASK_FOO=bar` is always processed before `FLASK_FOO__X=1`. After the flat key sets `self["FOO"] = "bar"`, the nested traversal does:

properties.body:
The `Blueprint` constructor explicitly prevents dots in names (`if "." in name: raise ValueError`) because dots denote nested blueprints. However, `app.register_blueprint(..., name="...")` doesn't enforce this check on the overridden name.

If a blueprint is registered with a dot via the `name` kwarg, it bypasses the restriction. This tricks the framework into treating it as a nested blueprint, causing the parent's callbacks (like `before_request`) to unexpectedly execute for the unrelated child blueprint.

### How to replicate the bug
```python
import flask

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
parent = flask.Blueprint("parent", __name__)
child = flask.Blueprint("child", __name__)

parent.before_request(lambda: setattr(flask.g, "hit", True))
child.add_url_rule("/", "index", lambda: str(hasattr(flask.g, "hit")))

app.register_blueprint(parent)
app.register_blueprint(child, name="parent.fake") # Bypasses dot validation

print(app.test_client().get("/").get_data(as_text=True))
properties.title: register_blueprint name override bypasses dot validation

properties.body: It's not bypassing anything. Registering on the app must allow dots, otherwise the nested names with dots couldn't be registered. As you've noticed, dispatch and the child relationship is based on the name, regardless of how it's registered. That's just how it works. `parent.register_blueprint(child)` is a shortcut for that.

Markdown
On Python versions prior to 3.11, `_CollectErrors.raise_any()` (in `src/flask/helpers.py`, line 682) only re-raises the very first collected error, silently swallowing any subsequent teardown errors. This makes debugging secondary teardown failures impossible on Python < 3.11.

### How to replicate the bug
1. Create a `_CollectErrors` context manager.
2. Trigger multiple teardown exceptions (e.g., DB close fails, then Cache flush fails).
3. Call `raise_any()`. Only the first exception is raised; the others are silently lost.

**Minimal Reproducible Example:**
```python
import sys

class _CollectErrors:
    def __init__(self):
        self.errors = []

    def __enter__(self):
        pass

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        if exc_val is not None:
            self.errors.append(exc_val)
        return True

    def raise_any(self, message: str) -> None:
        if self.errors:
            if sys.version_info >= (3, 11):
                raise BaseExceptionGroup(message, self.errors)
            else:
                raise self.errors[0]   # BUG: only first error raised

collect = _CollectErrors()

with collect:
    raise RuntimeError("DB connection close failed")
with collect:
    raise ValueError("File handle close failed")

try:
    collect.raise_any("Teardown errors")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    print(f"Total collected: {len(collect.errors)}")
```

Expected behavior
Even without BaseExceptionGroup (which is 3.11+), subsequent errors should not be silently discarded. They should ideally be chained or at least logged before raising the first error.

Proposed Fix
Consider chaining the exceptions or logging the secondary ones before raising the first on Python versions < 3.11.

Environment:

Python version: < 3.11 (e.g., 3.10)

Flask version: 3.2.0.dev (flask-main branch)

## Summary

Avoid subscripted `click.ParamType[...]` at runtime for the `flask run --cert` option type, while preserving the generic base for static type checking.

## Root cause

`CertParamType` inherited from `click.ParamType[str | os.PathLike[str] | ssl.SSLContext]`. That expression is evaluated when `flask.cli` is imported. With Flask's minimum Click version, `ParamType` is not subscriptable at runtime; with newer Click, the expression also requires `ssl` at runtime. Both cases can break `import flask` before any CLI command runs.

## What

`Config.from_file()` was missing `errno.ENOTDIR` from its silent error check, making it behave inconsistently with `Config.from_pyfile()`.

**Before (from_file):**
```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
    return False
```

**After (from_file):**
```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
    return False
```

`from_pyfile()` has always included `errno.ENOTDIR` in this check.

## Why it matters

`ENOTDIR` is raised when a path component in the given filename is a regular file rather than a directory (e.g. trying to open `/some/file/config.json` where `/some/file` is a regular file). With `silent=True`, callers expect all "file not accessible" errors to be swallowed and `False` returned. The missing code caused an unexpected `OSError` to bubble up instead.

Fixes #6023

## Summary

`Config.from_file()` and `Config.from_pyfile()` behave inconsistently when `silent=True` and an `OSError` is raised.

`from_pyfile()` silences errors for these `errno` codes:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
    return False
```

But `from_file()` only silences:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
    return False
```

It is missing `errno.ENOTDIR`.

## Reproduction

`ENOTDIR` is raised when a path component is a regular file, not a directory. For example, if `/tmp/myconfig` is a regular file and you try to open `/tmp/myconfig/settings.json`, the OS raises `ENOTDIR` (not a directory).

```python
import os, tempfile
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# create a file where we expect a directory
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False, suffix="cfg") as f:
    f.write(b"")
    tmp = f.name

# from_pyfile with silent=True returns False (correct)
result = app.config.from_pyfile(tmp + "/nested.cfg", silent=True)
# from_file with silent=True raises OSError instead of returning False (bug)
result = app.config.from_file(tmp + "/nested.json", load=json.load, silent=True)
```

## Expected behavior

Both methods should return `False` when `silent=True` and the path is not reachable due to `ENOTDIR`, just like they both return `False` for `ENOENT` and `EISDIR`.

## Fix

Add `errno.ENOTDIR` to the tuple in `from_file()`:

```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
    return False
```

## Summary

Adds a `RuntimeWarning` when Flask's development server is bound to a non-localhost address. The Werkzeug debugger allows arbitrary code execution when exposed to the network, yet many tutorials and quick-start guides instruct users to bind to `0.0.0.0` without warning them of the risks.

## Security Impact

Binding the Werkzeug development server to a non-localhost address while debug mode is enabled exposes the interactive debugger to the network. The debugger's PIN-protected console can execute arbitrary Python code. This change warns users when:

1. The host is set to a non-local address (anything other than `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, or `::1`)
2. Debug mode is additionally enabled — an escalated warning for the most dangerous configuration

## Implementation

- Uses `warnings.warn()` with `RuntimeWarning` so the warning is visible but doesn't prevent the server from starting
- Uses `stacklevel=2` so the warning points to the user's `app.run()` call, not the internal implementation
- No breaking changes — existing behavior is preserved; the warning is advisory

This aligns with the Google Patch Rewards qualifying submissions: "Elimination of error-prone design patterns or library calls." Binding a debug-capable server to 0.0.0.0 without warnings is a well-known footgun that has led to real-world compromises.

`kumquat`

- [x] No breaking changes to existing behavior
- [x] Uses standard library `warnings` module (no new dependencies)
- [x] Warning points to correct caller location via `stacklevel`
- [x] Compatible with all Python versions Flask supports

# Improve error messages when after_request hooks forget to return response

## Summary

This PR adds validation in the `process_response` method to detect when `after_request` hooks return `None` and raise an immediate, descriptive error. Previously, returning `None` from an `after_request` hook would silently set the response to `None`, causing a cryptic `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable` later during WSGI response delivery. Now users get a clear message identifying the offending hook by name.

## Root Cause

The `process_response` method in `src/flask/app.py` calls each `after_request` function and reassigns the response variable to its return value without validation. When a hook returns `None` (e.g., `lambda _: None`), the response becomes `None`. This error only surfaces later in `wsgi_app` when Flask attempts to call `response(environ, start_response)`, producing an unhelpful error message that doesn't indicate an `after_request` hook is responsible.

## Changes Made

Modified the `process_response` method in `src/flask/app.py` to validate the return value of each `after_request` function. After calling each hook, we now check if the return value is `None` and raise a `TypeError` with a descriptive message that includes the hook's function name. This validation applies to all `after_request` functions across both the app and blueprint scopes.

## Testing

All 487 existing tests pass with this change. The fix provides immediate feedback at the point of failure, making debugging significantly easier for users who accidentally omit a return statement in their `after_request` hooks.

## Problem

The open_resource method joins the user-provided 'resource' parameter with root_path using os.path.join without sanitizing for path traversal sequences (e.g., '../'). If a developer passes user-controlled input to this method, it could allow reading arbitrary files on the filesystem.

**Severity**: `low`

Add path traversal validation by resolving the final path and checking it is still within root_path: resolved = os.path.realpath(path); if not resolved.startswith(os.path.realpath(self.root_path)): raise ValueError('Path traversal detected').

I noticed a real crash path in session saving: `SecureCookieSessionInterface.save_session` called `dumps()` on `get_signing_serializer(app)` without checking whether the serializer existed.

I validated the behavior locally with a minimal reproduction where a session object was present, then `app.secret_key` became falsy before save. In that flow, Flask raised an internal `AttributeError` (`'NoneType' object has no attribute 'dumps'`) instead of the normal session configuration error.

Then I fixed the code in a streamlined way:

- I added a guard in `save_session` to handle a missing serializer explicitly.
- I raised the same user-facing `RuntimeError` message Flask already uses for missing secret key session failures.
- I removed the `type: ignore[union-attr]` usage by handling the union properly.
- I deduplicated the error message by using a shared constant for both `NullSession` and `save_session`.

After that, I added a focused regression test that reproduces the exact scenario:

- Start with a valid secret key.
- Create a modified session.
- Clear the secret key.
- Call `save_session` and assert Flask raises the expected runtime error message.

I also made sure the patch stayed minimal and clean:

- Only two files are changed:
  - `src/flask/sessions.py`
  - `tests/test_session_interface.py`

Bad Request

``` seems to be related to https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/pull/3113/changes#diff-32b889e713f9b5346cff198fd82aabe162ae8c529f008fa2a7a8fc6dbff17570L98 Note: in our case it is the underscore allowed in docker service names but no longer in werkzeug 3.1.7 Allo hostnames now need to comply with the [regex](https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/pull/3113/changes#diff-32b889e713f9b5346cff198fd82aabe162ae8c529f008fa2a7a8fc6dbff17570R11): ```python _host_re = re.compile( r""" ( [a-z0-9.-]+ # domain or ipv4 | \[[a-f0-9]*:[a-f0-9.:]+] # ipv6 ) (?::[0-9]+)? # optional port """, flags=re.ASCII | re.IGNORECASE | re.VERBOSE, ) ```

That test is just wrong, the `Host` header should only contain ASCII.

Hostnames cannot have underscores. That needs to be reported as a bug to Docker Compose, regardless of if we change anything in Werkzeug.

Change the default value of `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` from `None` to `"Lax"`.

When set to `None`, Flask does not include the `SameSite` attribute on session cookies, relying on browser defaults. While modern browsers default to `Lax` behavior when the attribute is absent, setting it explicitly ensures consistent CSRF defense-in-depth across all browser versions, including older ones that do not apply the `Lax` default.

Django has defaulted to `"Lax"` since 2.1 (2018). Express.js and Rails also default to `Lax`. This aligns Flask with the ecosystem standard.

Applications that require cross-site cookie behavior can set `SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE` to `None` (with `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True`).

All existing tests pass with this change (486 passed, 0 regressions).

## Description

`Config.from_file()` is missing `errno.ENOTDIR` in its silent error handling, while `Config.from_pyfile()` correctly includes it.

When a component of the config file path is a regular file rather than a directory (e.g., trying to load `file/config.json` where `file` is a regular file), `from_file(silent=True)` raises an `OSError` instead of silently returning `False`.

This inconsistency was originally reported in #5912.

## Changes

- **src/flask/config.py**: Added `errno.ENOTDIR` to the error check in `from_file()`, matching the existing behavior of `from_pyfile()` (line 211).
- **tests/test_config.py**: Added `test_config_from_file_not_a_directory` to verify the fix.

## Before

```python
# from_pyfile (line 211) - correct
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):

# from_file (line 296) - missing ENOTDIR
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
```

## After

Both methods now handle the same errno values consistently.

## Description

The `examples/celery/README.md` does not mention that **Redis is required** 
as a message broker for Celery to work. A beginner following the instructions 
will successfully start the Celery worker but immediately see repeated 
connection errors like:
```
ERROR/MainProcess] consumer: Cannot connect to redis://localhost:6379//:

This is confusing because nothing in the README warns about this dependency.

4. Nothing in the README explains why or how to fix it

The README should mention that Redis is required and provide 
setup instructions for it.

Add the following before the `celery` run command in `README.md`:
```rst
Celery requires a message broker. Install and start Redis before 
running the worker:

$ sudo apt install redis-server   # Debian/Ubuntu
$ sudo service redis start

# Verify Redis is running:
$ redis-cli ping
# Expected output: PONG
```

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu / Debian (Linux)
- Flask version: latest (main branch)
- Celery version: 5.6.2

## Additional Notes

This is a documentation-only change with no impact on code. 
It improves the onboarding experience for beginners on 
Debian/Ubuntu systems, which are the most common Linux distributions.

properties.body:
Modern browsers normalize backslashes in navigation URLs (e.g., `\\evil.com`) into forward slashes (`//evil.com`). This creates a discrepancy between how Flask/Werkzeug evaluates redirect targets and how user agents ultimately interpret them.

A common pattern used by Flask developers to prevent protocol-relative redirects is:

```python
if not url.startswith("//"):
    return redirect(url)
```

However, the following payload bypasses this logic:

```
\\evil.com
```

Flask/Werkzeug evaluates this as a safe relative path (`startswith("//") == False`), while browsers normalize it to:

```
https://evil.com
```

and perform an external redirect. This normalization behavior is consistent across Chrome, Firefox, and Safari.

As Flask does not provide a built-in redirect validation helper, developers routinely implement ad-hoc string checks that do not account for browser normalization rules, resulting in an ecosystem-wide class of open-redirect flaws.

**Feature Request**

Introduce an official, browser-aware redirect safety utility in Flask or Werkzeug, similar to Django’s `is_safe_url`, to standardize redirect validation across the framework. The helper should:

1. Normalize backslashes to forward slashes before validation.
2. Reject protocol-relative URLs (`//example.com`).
3. Optionally enforce allowed host checks.
4. Provide a documented, recommended pattern for safe redirects.

**Rationale**

- This issue is not a flaw in Flask’s redirect implementation but a recurring security footgun for developers due to inconsistent handling between application logic and browser URL normalization.
- Providing an official helper reduces the likelihood of open-redirect vulnerabilities in applications built on Flask.
- This is framework hardening rather than a security bug report, and it aligns with the expectations set by other frameworks that offer standardized redirect-safety utilities.

This feature would give developers a reliable and recommended approach to validating redirect targets securely, reducing reliance on fragile custom logic.
properties.title: Add a built-in is_safe_redirect() helper to handle browser URL normalization (backslash → forward slash)

Description
Flask currently parses JSON input using json.loads() without providing an application-level mechanism to enforce payload size limits or preprocess raw JSON before deserialization.
This feature would introduce configuration settings such as:
•⁠  ⁠JSON_MAX_STRING_LENGTH – to reject JSON payloads exceeding a defined size before parsing.
•⁠  ⁠JSON_PREPROCESS_RAW – to allow an optional callable to preprocess raw JSON text before json.loads() is executed.

Example of the Problem This Would Resolve
If a client sends a very large JSON payload (for example, 15–20MB), Flask will attempt to parse it entirely in memory. This can lead to unnecessary memory consumption and CPU usage, especially in API-heavy environments. While infrastructure-level limits (e.g., reverse proxies) may mitigate this, application-level safeguards provide defense-in-depth and improve reliability.
Currently, this problem can only be addressed by subclassing JSONProvider, overriding loads(), or modifying framework internals. Providing built-in configuration support would make it easier to enforce consistent JSON parsing policies without custom framework patches.
properties.title: Add configurable JSON parsing limits and preprocessing hook

In `AppContext.pop()`, if `do_teardown_appcontext` raises an exception, `_cv_app.reset()` and the context token cleanup are skipped. This leaves the context variable in a corrupted state, which can cause subsequent operations to see stale context data.

Similarly, if `do_teardown_request` raises, `_request.close()` is not called, potentially leaking file handles from the request body.

This adds nested `try/finally` blocks to ensure:

- `_request.close()` runs even if `do_teardown_request` raises
- `_cv_app.reset()` and token cleanup run even if `do_teardown_appcontext` raises
- The `appcontext_popped` signal is always sent

While teardown functions should avoid raising exceptions per the documentation, the framework-level cleanup should still be guaranteed regardless.

The previous implementation used Werkzeug’s default PBKDF2 hashing and allowed weak passwords with no protection against brute-force login attempts.
I upgraded the system by implementing Argon2 password hashing, enforcing strong password validation rules, adding login rate limiting to prevent brute-force attacks, and securing session cookies with proper security configurations.
These improvements make the authentication flow closer to production-level security while keeping the existing functionality intact.


1. Password Hashing
• Previous system used PBKDF2 via Werkzeug, suitable for learning projects.
• Upgraded to Argon2 hashing, which is more resistant to brute-force attacks and recommended
by modern security standards.
2. Password Strength Validation
• Earlier system allowed weak passwords without validation.
• New implementation enforces minimum length, uppercase, lowercase, numeric, and special
character requirements.
3. Brute-Force Protection
• Previously allowed unlimited login attempts.
• Now uses Flask Limiter to restrict login attempts (e.g., 5 per minute), preventing automated
attacks.
4. Session Security
• Default cookie configuration posed potential XSS and CSRF risks.
• Enabled secure cookie settings: Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite for safer session handling.
Final Outcome
• Authentication system is now production ready.
• Improved resistance against brute-force attacks, weak passwords, and session theft

properties.body: Werkzeug dev is failing because the duplicate check still needs to be fixed there. This fix here is related to that ongoing work.

While dealing with trying to detect duplicate routes in https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/issues/3105, I ran into an issue with Flask, which adds `OPTIONS` to every single rule by default.

I started looking into Flask's `provide_automatic_options` feature, and it's just weird.

- Why is there a `PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS` config? What benefit is there to turning `OPTIONS` off at all, let alone configuring it for a given deployment.
- Flask adds `OPTIONS` to every route, then has a check that runs on dispatching _every_ request to see if the method was `OPTIONS` and `provide_automatic_options` was enabled for the rule. Performing this check for every request seems wasteful, as opposed to adding an actual rule and endpoint so that the routing that's already happening handles it.
    - But adding a rule is also sort of bad, as it results in a bunch of duplicate rules since Flask has no way to know what other rules have already been added. This can be caught with Werkzeug 3.2, and doesn't cause problems in earlier versions, but it's still annoying.
- `provide_automatic_options` can be set as an attribute on the view function. There are some other attributes that are barely documented as well, such as `required_methods`. This is presumably mostly for `View` classes, but works on functions too, making type annotations unhelpful.
- If `PROVIDE_AUTOMATIC_OPTIONS` is disabled (not the default), the logic for the `provide_automatic_options` argument and attribute doesn't work correctly to _enable_ it, it only works for _disabling_.
- The tests for this were incomplete and had some issues. Some other tests were revealed to be adding duplicate rules as well. 

At a minimum I've fixed the enabling issue. I've also got a change that registers a route and view for options instead of using special dispatch logic. We should also consider deprecating the config.

By default, `@app.route` sets `methods` to support only `GET` requests and the [documentation](https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/api/#flask.Flask.route) suggests that the parameters are then passed to `Rule`, where `methods=None` allows all methods to be used. In reality, even explicit `None` is treated as a default value and gets overwritten by `["GET"]`. I suggest adding a way to allow all methods by explicitly passing `None`.

This feature would allow more direct control over `Rule` parameters when using `@app.route`, only using defaults when no value was provided. It is currently possible to work around the issue by creating the `Rule` directly, but it would be more convinient to have that option with `@app.route` decorators. It would also remove some confusion, as `None` being treated the same way as no value by `@app.route` while having a special meaning in `Rule` seems like a bug.

properties.body:
Unlike Werkzeug, Flask has a more structured approach to routes and endpoints. I'm currently dealing with routing stuff right now, and do not want to surface more of these options in Flask. Adding more options that change behavior on "not provided" vs "none" makes things more confusing to annotate and implement and reason about.

As you say, if you need this feature it's still possible to use, as Werkzeug's entire routing system is still available.

```python
def add_url_rule(app, rule, endpoint=None, view_func=None, **kwargs):
    if endpoint is None:
        endpoint = view_func.__name__

    app.url_map.add(app.url_rule_class(*args, endpoint=endpoint, **kwargs))

    if view_func is not None:
        app.view_funcs[endpoint] = view_func
```

You can also register it the normal way with `@app.route`, then remove the methods:

```python
for rule in app.url_map.iter_rules(endpoint):
    rule.methods = None
```

> Adding more options that change behavior on "not provided" vs "none" makes things more confusing to annotate and implement and reason about.

In that case, it might be helpful to add a line to the documentation that would make it clear that `None` in `@app.route` is treated as default value and is not passed to `Rule`.

## Summary

- `Config.from_file()` with `silent=True` raises `NotADirectoryError` when a path component is a regular file rather than a directory (e.g. `~/.myapp/config.json` when `~/.myapp` is a regular file). This is inconsistent with `Config.from_pyfile()`, which correctly handles this case by returning `False`.
- The root cause is that `errno.ENOTDIR` was added to `from_pyfile` in PR #2581 (fixing #2545) but was never applied to `from_json` (now `from_file`), even though the original issue title mentioned "from_json, etc."

properties.title: Fix Config.from_file() silent mode not handling ENOTDIR

properties.body:
## Description

`Config.from_file()` is missing `errno.ENOTDIR` in its silent error handling, while `Config.from_pyfile()` correctly includes it.

In `from_pyfile` (line ~193):
```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR, errno.ENOTDIR):
```

In `from_file` (line ~239):
```python
if silent and e.errno in (errno.ENOENT, errno.EISDIR):
```

The `ENOTDIR` case was added to `from_pyfile` in PR #2581 (fixing issue #2545), but the fix was never applied to `from_json` (now `from_file`), even though the original issue title mentioned "from_json, etc."

## Reproduction

When a component of the config file path is a regular file rather than a directory (e.g., `~/.myapp` is a file, and you try to load `~/.myapp/config.toml`), `from_file()` with `silent=True` raises `OSError` with `errno.ENOTDIR` instead of silently returning `False`.

```python
import flask
import tomllib

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
# If ~/.myapp is a regular file, this raises instead of returning False
app.config.from_file("~/.myapp/config.toml", load=tomllib.load, text=False, silent=True)
```

## Expected Behavior

`from_file(..., silent=True)` should return `False` when a path component is not a directory, matching the behavior of `from_pyfile(..., silent=True)`.

## Environment

- Flask version: 3.1.x / main branch

Ensure that `request.close()` is always executed even if
`do_teardown_request()` raises an exception.

Currently, if a user-defined teardown handler raises an exception,
`request.close()` is skipped, which can lead to resource leaks

This change wraps teardown execution in a `try/finally` block to
guarantee cleanup without altering normal behavior.
properties.title: Fix request resource leak when teardown handlers raise

properties.body:
From the docs: https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/reqcontext/#teardown-callbacks

> Be sure to write these functions in a way that does not depend on other callbacks and will not fail.

There are a lot more places than this in `pop` that could result in leftover state, which is why we warn that teardown functions must not fail. For example, if a teardown function fails, any remaining are not run. In that sense, `close` is just another teardown function. As to why the existing `finally` is there in that case, no idea.

@davidism 
I’m not trying to make teardown callbacks safe to fail , only to ensure that framework owned cleanup (request.close()) is not skipped when they do

What I'm saying is that adding a `finally` here doesn't really help, as any callback failing means that other resources are also potentially left dangling. In that case, the issue is with the callback, and needs to be fixed there.

I've been working on closing resources over in Werkzeug's tests, maybe that's what prompted you to look at this. I'm also working on that here, just haven't pushed the changes yet. Thanks for pointing out this area, if nothing else I'll move the appcontext teardown out of the `finally` and into the `try` so that the context is always cleared. Perhaps there's also a case for `try/except pass` around every teardown function, to clean up as much as possible, I'll look into that.

This is an internal, non-user-facing refactor.

The `make_response` method currently contains inline logic to unpack
response tuples with different valid shapes. While this logic is correct,
it is dense and increases cognitive load in an already large method.

Refactoring this logic into a small private helper would improve
readability and long-term maintainability without changing behavior.

The current tuple unpacking logic handles multiple valid forms
((body, status, headers), (body, status), (body, headers)) inline inside
`make_response`. This makes the control flow harder to follow and
duplicates validation responsibilities within the method.

This is not easily improved via subclassing or extensions, as the logic
is internal to Flask's response handling. A small internal refactor would
isolate this responsibility and make future maintenance safer.

I can't reproduce this with the information provided. Thanks for providing a minimal example, but it's still a bit all over the place.

You're still using the old `setup.py` pattern, rather than using `pyproject.toml` with a `[build-system]` section. ### Summary
`render_template_string` and `stream_template_string` now cache compiled templates, avoiding repeated compilation when the same source string is rendered multiple times.

The cache is stored per-app on the `Environment` instance with LRU eviction:
- `string_template_cache_size`: max 100 cached templates (configurable via class attribute)
- `string_template_cache_max_len`: templates longer than 100,000 characters are not cached

### Benchmark

The following script runs a server and computes how many requests can be received within 5 seconds.

```py
from threading import Thread
import requests, time, random
import sys
import os

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "src"))) # run this script within Flask's directory
from flask import Flask, request, render_template_string

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/template')
def t():
    return render_template_string('Hello, {{name}}',  name=request.args.get('q', ''))

def bench():
    time.sleep(1)  # wait for server
    n, end = 0, time.time() + 5
    s = requests.Session()
    while time.time() < end:
        s.get(f'http://127.0.0.1:6000/template?q={random.randint(0,10**6)}')
        n += 1
    print(f'\n{n} requests in 5s ({n/5:.0f} req/s)')
    import os; os._exit(0)

Thread(target=bench).start()
app.run(port=6000, threaded=True)
```

Without cache:
`5373 requests in 5s (1075 req/s)`

With cache:
`8603 requests in 5s (1721 req/s)`

8603/5373 = ~60% speed improvement

Stop using AI

Flask and Werkzeug `redirect` currently defaults to a [302](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/302). Routing uses [307](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/307) since that preserves method consistently. We didn't change the `redirect` default to 307, since that would break the common pattern of "GET form, POST form, redirect to GET result", ending up doing "POST result" instead. [303](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/303) seems designed exactly for this pattern, so that a redirect always results in a GET, instead of preserving the method or only rewriting it sometimes. [HTMX actually calls this out about Flask.](https://hypermedia.systems/htmx-patterns/#:~:text=cleaner%2E-,A,resource)

I don't _think_ there would actually be a problem switching to 303 as the default. It would still do the expected thing for basic page redirects and form submission redirects. I would be really surprised if anyone was relying on the 302 behavior of only converting POST and nothing else. I don't even remember that being the behavior when we were switching to 307, and I would have switched to 303 instead of leaving 302 then if I had known about it.

### Summary

At the moment, `teardown_request` handlers in Flask are synchronous and cannot be defined as async functions. This makes it harder for apps that depend on async cleanup logic (e.g., closing async DB connections or awaiting async tasks) to integrate cleanly with Flask’s request lifecycle.

### Problem

When users attempt to define an async teardown handler like:

```python
@app.teardown_request
async def cleanup_async_resources(response):
    await close_async_connections()
```

Flask does not await it and treats it as a regular function, leading to unawaited coroutine warnings and the async cleanup not running as intended.

### Proposed Solution
Make teardown handlers awaitable - if a handler is declared async, Flask should await it during the teardown phase.

### Example
```python
@app.teardown_request
async def cleanup_async_resources(response):
    await some_async_cleanup()  # should be awaited before response is finalized
```

### Motivation
Better async integration support as more frameworks and applications adopt async patterns. This would make Flask’s async support more complete and intuitive.

### Environment

```python
Flask version: (e.g., 3.2.x)
Python version: 3.9+
```

Async libs used: Any

### Thanks!

This PR adds documentation clarifying the limitations and unsupported nature of using Flask async views together with gevent monkey patching.

While simple async views may appear to work for individual requests, concurrent requests can fail due to conflicts between asyncio’s event loop assumptions and gevent’s greenlet-based threading model.
